notes.title: Introducing yourself when you meet someone

blocks.content: In the dialogue, Mali says ฉันชื่อมะลิค่ะ — "My name is Mali." — and asks คุณชื่ออะไรคะ — "What is your name?". Asking someone's name and giving your own name form a simple first-meeting exchange. For "I", a female speaker uses ฉัน, while a male speaker uses ผม.
[pronoun] + ชื่อ + [name] = giving your own name

examples.thai_script: ฉันชื่อฝนค่ะ
ผมชื่อนัทครับ

blocks.content: Narin then says ยินดีที่ได้รู้จักครับ — "Nice to meet you.". ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก is a fixed expression you can use when meeting someone for the first time. The expression itself stays the same; only the polite particle changes with the speaker.
Do not try to break ยินดีที่ได้รู้จัก into separate words yet. Learn it as one complete phrase for now — you will meet the individual words later.

notes.title: Speaking politely with ครับ, ค่ะ and คะ

blocks.content: In the dialogue, Mali says สวัสดีค่ะ — "Hello." — while Narin says สวัสดีครับ — "Hello.". Thai often marks politeness with a particle at the end of an utterance. A female speaker uses ค่ะ in a statement, while a male speaker uses ครับ.
[statement] + ค่ะ / ครับ = polite statement

For a female speaker, the polite ending changes with the sentence: ค่ะ is used for a statement, but คะ is used for a question. A male speaker uses ครับ for both statements and questions. Keeping these female forms separate is important because they are not interchangeable.
The first two are both said by a female speaker: only the ending changes with the type of sentence. The third shows a male speaker asking the same question.

examples.thai_script: ฉันชื่อฟ้าค่ะ
คุณชื่ออะไรคะ
คุณชื่ออะไรครับ

blocks.content: Pay attention to the tone difference between ค่ะ (kâ) and คะ (ká).
